definition: Surreptitious means done secretly so as not to be noticed.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word surreptitious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know surreptitious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: He perfected the surreptitious snack, easing the granola wrapper open inside his desk one silent millimeter at a time.
Discreet keeps a low profile out of tact—nothing needs hiding; surreptitious actively works to escape notice in the moment.
Undercover goes beyond surreptitious: a surreptitious act hides one deed, while an undercover officer hides a whole identity for months at a stretch.

Stealthy is about the body: moving softly and slowly so as not to be heard or seen, like a cat crossing gravel. Surreptitious is about the plan of an act — timed and placed to escape notice — and it needs no movement at all; a surreptitious payment never makes a sound.

Sneaky is the informal cousin, and it always smuggles in a whiff of guilt or bad intent — the sneaky shortcut, the sneaky bite of someone else's dessert. Surreptitious judges only the manner of an act, not its morals: a surreptitious deed can be perfectly kind, so long as it is carried out to escape notice.

For two weeks the crew planned the captain's retirement surprise with surreptitious care: decorations came aboard in grocery boxes, rehearsals ran during her watch, and the banner was sewn in the engine room—the one compartment she never visited.
Surreptitious describes the manner of a single act: done under someone's nose, timed and placed to escape notice.
The act itself can be innocent—a surprise party qualifies—which separates the word from plain 'sneaky,' with its whiff of guilt.
Surreptitious is the manner word in this unit's hiding cluster: it describes how a particular act is carried out—quietly, under watchful eyes, timed to escape notice.
Conceal names what you do to the thing; secretive names a person's standing habit; evasive names the dodge when questions come.
The act itself can be guilty or perfectly kind.

Every catalog in the county listed the Harmon branch library as having no budget for repairs, and every winter more spines cracked.
Yet somehow the damage never grew.
Torn atlases reappeared rebound; a children's encyclopedia lost its water stains.
Okafor, was responsible, though no one knew it.
His repairs were surreptitious by design: done between rounds at two in the morning, glue and clamps packed away before the first librarian arrived.
He wanted no thanks and no questions about where the materials came from -- he bought them himself.
It took a burst pipe and an emergency inventory for anyone to notice that half the collection had been quietly mended by hands nobody had ever seen at work.
